nature-res-107.title: Land use: what people do with every patch of ground
nature-res-107.text: Barely a tenth of Earth's land surface is arable, fit for plowing and planting: 10.7% as of 2015, with another 1.3% under permanent crops. The rest does other jobs. Land use is the name for those jobs. It describes what happens on a piece of land, both the benefits people get from it and the management they carry out there. The IPCC, the United Nations' climate science panel, sorts land into six groups: forest land, cropland, grassland, wetlands, settlements and other lands. The choice matters far beyond the plot itself. Land use strongly affects water, soil, nutrients, plants and animals, which makes it a large part of {{ref:nature-eco-129}}. Its side effects include urban sprawl, soil erosion, land degradation and desertification. To avoid clashes between uses that do not fit side by side, governments often plan and regulate land use, for example by zoning.

nature-res-131.title: Forestry: the craft of growing and using forests
nature-res-131.text: Forests provide more than 86 million green jobs, and an estimated 880 million people collect firewood or make charcoal. The field that looks after them is forestry: the science and craft of creating, managing, planting, using, conserving and repairing forests and woodlands. Its practitioner is a forester, who works in plantations and in natural stands. Modern forestry practices multiple-use management, balancing timber, fuel wood, wildlife habitat, water quality, recreation and jobs. The narrower job of managing forests for timber is {{ref:nature-res-156}}, though the two words are often used as synonyms. Policy has tended to favor benefits that sell, like timber. That bias has prompted frameworks that also count the non-market ecosystem services forests provide. The human stakes are large. Some 252 million people living in forests and savannahs earn less than US$1.25 a day. The work itself is dangerous: in the United States, logging has a fatality rate 30 times higher than all other occupations.

nature-res-092.title: Running a forest: the business side of forestry
nature-res-092.text: In 2025, 1.20 billion hectares of forest, 29% of all the world's forest, was managed mainly for wood and non-wood products. About 616 million hectares more was designated for multiple use. Forest management is the branch of forestry that runs these places. It handles the administrative, legal, economic and social side, along with technical work such as {{ref:nature-res-156}} and forest protection. A forest can be managed for timber, recreation, water, wildlife, wood products or {{ref:nature-gov-046}}, aiming at conservation, use or a mix of both. The tools include extracting timber, planting and replanting, building roads and paths, and preventing fire. Intensity ranges from leaving a forest alone to intensive timber-growing regimes, chosen to meet economic or ecological goals. What forests give back is broad: water, slower climate change, shelter for pollinators, timber, fuelwood, food, medicine and rural livelihoods. Some forests are still run only for firewood, paper fiber and timber. Managing for several uses at once is becoming more common as environmental awareness grows. Modern scientific forestry arose from the 1750s in France and German-speaking countries. It rested on central management by professional foresters and on sustainable yield.

nature-res-133.title: Groundwater, the planet's buried store of fresh water
nature-res-133.text: About 99% of the world's liquid fresh water lies underground. This groundwater fills the pore spaces of soil and rock, and the cracks in rock, beneath Earth's surface. At a certain depth, called the water table, soil or rock becomes completely saturated. In the {{ref:nature-eco-196}}, water soaking down from the surface recharges it, and it flows back out naturally at springs and seeps. People lean on it heavily. Groundwater supplies about half of the world's drinking water, 40% of irrigation water and a third of industrial water. It makes up about 30 percent of readily available fresh water. It also works as natural storage, a buffer when surface water runs short in drought. Some of it is ancient: deep water that soaked in millennia ago is called fossil water. Not all of it is drinkable, because arsenic, fluoride and salt can contaminate it.

nature-res-101.title: Water resources: why a wet planet runs short
nature-res-101.text: About 97% of Earth's water is salt water. Only 3% is fresh, and slightly over two-thirds of that is frozen in glaciers and ice caps. Water resources are the natural sources of water that could be useful to people, for drinking, irrigation or other needs. They are one kind of natural resource. Most fresh water that is not frozen lies underground as groundwater, with only a small fraction above ground or in the air. Natural sources include surface water, water flowing beneath rivers, groundwater and ice. People add artificial sources too: reclaimed wastewater, desalinated seawater with the salt removed, harvested rainwater, wells, dams and reservoirs. A surface water system has only one natural input, the precipitation that falls on the land draining into it, part of the {{ref:nature-eco-196}}. Climate change is shifting that balance. It brings heavier rain and floods, while droughts can shrink groundwater storage and the recharge that refills it.

nature-res-088.title: Water scarcity: enough water, wrong place, wrong time
nature-res-088.text: Half a billion people live with severe water scarcity all year, and around four billion face it for at least one month a year. Yet the planet as a whole has enough fresh water. Water scarcity is a lack of fresh water sources, local or affordably brought in, to meet a region's normal demand. It is a form of {{ref:nature-found-051}}, and its root is a mismatch between when and where people need water and when and where it is available. Of the 1.4 billion cubic kilometers of water on Earth, the UN estimates only 200,000 cubic kilometers is fresh water available for people. Experts distinguish two types, {{ref:nature-res-089}} and {{ref:nature-res-090}}. Many forces drive it: population growth, changing diets and living conditions, expanding irrigated farming, climate change, deforestation, water pollution and wasteful use. The main consumption-driven cause is heavy water use in agriculture, livestock breeding and industry. Responses range from managing supply and demand to cooperation between countries, conservation, reusing wastewater and desalination. In 2019 the World Economic Forum named water scarcity one of the largest global risks by potential impact over the next decade.

nature-res-119.title: Drainage basins: where the rain is headed
nature-res-119.text: The Amazon basin covers 7 million km2, and all the water flowing across its surface heads for one river mouth. A drainage basin is an area of land where all flowing surface water drains to one point, such as a river mouth, lake or ocean. North Americans call it a watershed; others say catchment or river basin. Ridges and hills form the drainage divide between one basin and the next. Most water leaving a basin's outlet fell on it as precipitation and ran off as {{ref:nature-eco-275}}. On the way it carries nutrients, sediment and pollutants, and {{ref:nature-nbs-268}} can cause eutrophication at the outlet. Because basins hang together as coherent units, water is commonly managed basin by basin. A basin that crosses a political border holds a transboundary river, managed jointly by the countries sharing it. After the Amazon, the largest basins are the Congo and the Nile.

nature-res-112.title: Aquifers: not underground lakes, but soaked rock
nature-res-112.text: An aquifer is not an underground river or lake. It is a layer of porous, permeable or fractured rock, or of gravel, sand or silt, saturated with groundwater. Porous means full of tiny spaces; permeable means water can move through them. People tap aquifers through wells for drinking water, farming and industry. Between aquifers may lie an aquitard, a layer of clay or non-porous rock that restricts groundwater flow. Trouble starts when people take out more water than nature puts back. That exceeds the aquifer's practical sustained yield, the amount it can supply year after year. The results include {{ref:nature-res-137}}, sinking land, creeping salt and polluted groundwater. The Ogallala Aquifer shows the scale: in its arid parts, annual recharge is only about 10 percent of annual withdrawals.

nature-res-140.title: Intensive farming: more food from every hectare
nature-res-140.text: Most of the meat, dairy, eggs, fruit and vegetables in a supermarket come from intensive farms. Intensive farming grows crops or raises animals with high inputs and outputs per unit of land, as opposed to extensive farming. It leaves little land fallow, or resting, and adds more capital, labor, farm chemicals and water to raise yields per hectare. Its roots go deep. From the 16th to 19th centuries, {{ref:nature-res-191}}, mechanization, {{ref:nature-nbs-278}} and selective breeding drove a rise in Britain's farm productivity. The costs travel far. Crop irrigation accounts for 70% of the world's fresh water use, and industrial agriculture causes 14–28% of net greenhouse gas emissions. Nitrogen from Midwest farms flows down the Mississippi and creates dead zones in the Gulf of Mexico. Yet intensity can also spare land. Raising productivity sustainably, especially on small farms, can reduce the land farming needs and slow deforestation.

nature-res-169.title: Water security: enough clean water, risks kept low
nature-res-169.text: About 27% of the world's population lived in water-scarce areas in the mid-2010s, a share likely to reach 42% by 2050. Water security is the goal that trend threatens. It means getting the most benefit from water for people and ecosystems while keeping the risks of floods, droughts and polluted water acceptably low. People with high water security always have enough water of acceptable quality for health, livelihoods and production. The concept emerged in the 21st century and is broader than the absence of water scarcity, although some organizations use it only for supply. Its main threats are scarcity, pollution, poorer water quality from climate change, poverty, destructive floods and natural disasters. How easily a society stays secure depends on its water environment, its economy and society, and future climate change. The IPCC predicted that 2 °C of global warming would expose roughly 1–4 billion people to water stress. Responses include engineering for more supply or efficiency, financial safety nets for poorer people and caps on demand. There is no standard way to measure it.

nature-res-125.title: The food system: from field to fork to bin
nature-res-125.text: Since 1961, food supply per person has risen by more than 30%. Behind that rise stands the food system: all the connected people, institutions, policies and infrastructure involved in feeding a population. It covers production, processing, packaging, distribution, marketing, eating and the disposal of food waste. Conventional food systems cut unit costs through economies of scale, the savings of producing in bulk, along with specialization, long supply chains and global trade. They depend heavily on cheap fossil fuels for machinery, fertilizer and processing. The results cut both ways. These systems raised productivity and food availability, supporting {{ref:nature-es-108}}. They are also linked to soil degradation, biodiversity loss and unequal access to food. And the food system causes more than a third (34%) of global greenhouse gas emissions.

nature-res-156.title: Silviculture: growing trees as a crop
nature-res-156.text: In 16th-century Germany, landowners facing deforestation developed a new discipline: silviculture. It is the practice of controlling how forests grow, what they are made of and their quality, mainly to produce timber. Forestry is the broad field; silviculture works at the level of the stand, a single group of trees. At heart it is the commercial business of growing forest crops, built on knowledge of how trees and stands live. A new crop can come from self-sown seed, sown seed or planted seedlings. Tending follows: spacing, pruning and thinning trees, or weeding out competing plants. Pruning has a clear payoff. Removing lower branches lets clear, knot-free wood grow, which is worth more. It does not always pay, though. On old, poor soils, or where dry-season fires threaten the crop, trees may grow too slowly.

nature-res-098.title: LULUCF: counting the carbon from land and forests
nature-res-098.text: Over 2014–2023, land use, land-use change and forestry released an average of 1.1 ± 0.7 Gt of carbon a year, or 4.1 ± 2.6 Gt of carbon dioxide. A Gt, or gigatonne, is a billion tonnes. These emissions get their own line in greenhouse gas accounts, a sector known as LULUCF. It covers emissions and removals from direct human land use, changes in land use, and forestry. Such activities can add carbon dioxide to the atmosphere or take it out. UN climate guidelines require countries to report human-caused emissions in six sectors, and LULUCF is one. The {{ref:nature-clim-056}} made accounting for planting and clearing forests mandatory, but accounting for forest, cropland and grazing management voluntary. Changing land also alters how much sunlight the ground reflects and evapotranspiration, the water soil and plants release into the air. Both affect climate. A 2021 study found that changes in use touched 17% of land in 1960–2019, with global trade a main driver.

nature-res-123.title: Food loss and waste: a third of the harvest, thrown away
nature-res-123.text: About one-third of the world's food is thrown away, wasting all the resources used to produce it. Food loss and waste is food lost or discarded without being eaten. It happens at every stage of the food system, but most food waste arises after consumers buy food. Global food waste comes to 931 million tonnes a year, about 121 kg per person. Households produce 61 percent, food service 26 percent and retail 13 percent. The climate bill is 3.3 billion tons of CO2-equivalent emissions a year, and landfilled food is a major methane source. Definitions vary. The FAO calls it a decrease in the quantity or quality of food along the supply chain, and bodies draw the line between loss and waste differently. Cutting waste brings social gains, such as productivity, food security and lower environmental impact, that individual actors may not take into account. The UN's {{ref:nature-gov-010}} aim to halve per capita retail and consumer food waste by 2030.

nature-res-115.title: Clearcutting: felling a whole forest at once
nature-res-115.text: The most economically efficient way to log is to take everything. Clearcutting cuts down most or all of the trees in an area at once, and it is also used to clear land for farming. The contrast is selective logging, which harvests only a few trees per hectare. A clearcut mimics the start of regrowth after a fire or windthrow, when wind blows trees down. The {{ref:nature-eco-348}} that follows favors fast-growing, sun-loving species. Bare land holds less water, which can worsen flooding and wash nutrients out of the soil. One study found nearly three times the erosion from slides in clear-cut zones, about five times once logging roads were counted. Its long-run effects depend on how well the forest is managed and whether the land is converted to other uses. Whether it is acceptable remains fiercely disputed. Loggers and forest-worker unions defend it on scientific, safety and economic grounds. Critics call it deforestation that destroys habitat, and the costs of topsoil loss are intensely debated.

nature-res-146.title: Pastoralism: herding where crops cannot grow
nature-res-146.text: Between 200 million and 500 million people practiced pastoralism as of 2019, and 75% of all countries had pastoral communities. Pastoralism raises livestock by letting animals graze on large open pastures, historically by nomads who moved with their herds. It is practiced where dryness, poor soils, extreme temperatures or lack of water make crops difficult or impossible. Pastoralists manage rangelands covering about a third of Earth's land surface, producing food where crops cannot grow. Mobility varies. Some herders make short daily moves, some practice transhumance between seasonal pastures, and some are fully nomadic. Fences, harder borders, spreading crop farming and the {{ref:nature-res-191}} of common land have made settled herding more common. One review of many studies found pastoralism 2 to 10 times more productive per unit of land than capital-intensive alternatives. Yet policies often try to replace it. Grazing can help keep savannas and woodlands diverse and stop them turning into dense shrubland or forest. Because they work marginal land, pastoral communities are very vulnerable to global warming.

nature-res-155.title: Shifting cultivation: farm a plot, then let it rest
nature-res-155.text: Shifting cultivation was one of the first forms of farming, and it is still widespread in the tropical developing world. A farmer crops a plot for a while, then leaves it to regrow wild vegetation and moves on. Land is often cleared by {{ref:nature-res-160}}, and after two or three years of crops the plot is left for another. Cropping usually stops when the soil tires or, more often, when weeds take over. The fallow, the resting period, usually lasts longer than the cropping. Fallows are not idle. They supply timber, firewood, medicines and game, and tree fallows protect soil from erosion and lift nutrients from deep layers. Fast population growth and outside economic change, such as chain saws and cash crops, have shortened fallows and lengthened cropping. Blame for tropical forest loss is disputed. Shifting cultivators are often accused, but some sources argue it comes from the forces that cleared Europe's forests: urbanization, industrialization, affluence and population growth. When the FAO named shifting cultivation, but not logging, as a cause of deforestation, it clashed with environmental groups.

nature-res-160.title: Slash-and-burn: fertilizing a field with fire
nature-res-160.text: Roughly 200–300 million people worldwide farm by slash-and-burn, a method in use since Neolithic times. It is a form of shifting cultivation in which forest or woodland plants are cut and burned to make a field, called a swidden. The cut vegetation dries and is set alight. The nutrient-rich ash fertilizes the soil and briefly clears weeds and pests. After about three to five years the nutrients run down and weeds and pests invade, so farmers move on. Recovery takes from five to more than twenty years. On the very poor, leached soils of places like the Amazon, it is one of the few kinds of farming possible. There it has been sustainable for thousands of years. But it works only with a huge amount of land or few people, and it suits cash crops poorly. It has become a common, and less sustainable, method of agricultural deforestation. Replacing it with {{ref:nature-clim-179}} could offset up to 12% of human carbon emissions from changing land use each year, some 0.21 gigatonnes.

nature-res-137.title: Groundwater depletion: pumping faster than it refills
nature-res-137.text: During the 20th century, the United States drew down about 800 cubic kilometers of its groundwater. That is groundwater depletion, also called overdrafting: pumping water from an aquifer faster than its equilibrium yield, the rate at which it stays in balance. Excessive pumping is the main cause, and too little recharge makes the aquifer less useful. Two limits guide managers. Safe yield is what can be withdrawn without exceeding long-term recharge. Sustainable yield also accounts for the effects on surface water. The damage starts at each well. Pumping creates a cone of depression, a funnel-shaped dip in the water table around the well, that widens as extraction goes on. Across a region the water table falls. Streams, wetlands and lakes shrink, the ground can subside, and salt water can push in. Farms are the main driver. Roughly 40% of global irrigation relies on groundwater, and irrigation is the main cause of storage loss in the US. It is a form of {{ref:nature-eco-063}}. Remedies include artificial recharge, better governance, incentives to conserve and more efficient farming.

nature-res-143.title: Land value tax: taxing the ground, not the building
nature-res-143.text: Most taxes discourage something useful. A property tax rises when an owner builds or repairs, so it discourages both. A land value tax avoids that trap by taxing the value of land alone, ignoring buildings and other improvements. Many economists favor it, arguing that it causes no economic inefficiency and helps reduce inequality. Because the amount of land is fixed, the tax cannot be passed on to tenants, consumers or workers. Its {{ref:nature-pol-128}} falls on landowners, who tend to be rich. It also removes the reward for holding unused land just to wait for its price to rise, freeing land for productive use. Evasion is hard, since land cannot be hidden or moved abroad and titles are publicly registered. Supporters add that land value comes from its surroundings, not from anything the owner does. Adam Smith first analyzed the tax rigorously in 1776, and Henry George later campaigned for a single tax on land to replace all others. It needs a land valuation and a title register, and it is impractical where titles and tenure are uncertain.

nature-res-129.title: Forest products: wood, paper and a global trade
nature-res-129.text: In 2023, global exports of wood and paper products were worth US$482 billion. A forest product is any material taken from forestry for direct use or sale, such as lumber, paper or livestock fodder. Wood is by far the main one, used as fuel, building material and pulp for paper. Industrial roundwood removals, the logs cut for industry, came to 1.92 billion cubic meters, and sawnwood production to 445 million cubic meters. Everything else a forest yields falls under {{ref:nature-res-174}}, seen as gentler on forests while giving local income. Wood products store carbon, and timber can replace concrete as a recyclable building material. Burning wood for energy is another matter. Bioenergy initially emits more greenhouse gas per unit of energy than fossil fuels, and regrowing trees takes decades or centuries to reabsorb it. Access restrictions, harvesting fees and harvest limits shape the economics of the trade.

nature-res-174.title: Non-timber forest products: nuts, mushrooms and medicine
nature-res-174.text: More than 28,000 plant species are recorded as medicinal, many of them from forests. They belong to a vast class of non-timber forest products: the useful foods, materials and goods taken from forests other than timber. The list includes game, nuts, berries, mushrooms, oils, sap, medicinal plants, fuelwood, fish, insects, spices and forage, harvested wild or farmed. Around 1 billion people depend to some extent on wild foods, and several million households rely on these products for income. A narrower subset, non-wood forest products, leaves out woodfuel and charcoal; the FAO estimated these generated US$88 billion in 2011. The total value is hard to pin down, because no broad system tracks the hundreds of products involved. Research treats them as commodities that can make keeping forests pay. In some places they offer a route out of poverty. {{ref:nature-res-193}} often manages forests for income from both timber and these products.

nature-res-139.title: Illegal logging: timber taken outside the law
nature-res-139.text: More than half of global logging may be illegal. Illegal logging is harvesting, transporting, buying or selling timber in breach of the law. It includes cutting without permission, in {{ref:nature-gov-038}}s, of protected species or beyond agreed limits, often through corruption. In trade, fraudulent customs declarations, tax avoidance and fake certification are called wood laundering. Demand for raw materials, {{ref:nature-res-142}} and demand for cattle pasture drive it. Losses from public land alone exceed US$10 billion a year. Estimates need caution, though: governments tend to underestimate the problem while NGOs publish alarming figures. The damage spreads. Illegal logging drives deforestation and biodiversity loss, fosters corruption and tax evasion, and cuts producer countries' revenue. The EU's 2003 FLEGT Action Plan fights it mainly through Voluntary Partnership Agreements with timber-producing countries.

nature-res-168.title: Water rights: who may take water from a river
nature-res-168.text: Where water is plentiful and users are few, water rights are simple. In dry, irrigated regions they often lead to legal and physical conflict. A water right is a user's legal right to take and use water from a source such as a river, stream, pond or groundwater. It is a form of {{ref:nature-econ-621}}. Often the right rests on owning the land the water touches, known as {{ref:nature-res-154}}, and is judged by a test of reasonable use. Where water is scarcer, as in the western United States, rights follow {{ref:nature-res-151}}: first in time, first in right. Each such right has an annual yield and a date, and it keeps that date when sold. The idea is old. In ancient Rome people could gain temporary rights to running water that did not depend on owning land and lasted while use continued. Over time rights broadened from land-based to use-based, letting non-landowners hold enforceable rights to clean water. Some systems treat surface water and groundwater alike; others apply different rules to each.

openers.forests-land-and-water: Every piece of land does a job, whether it grows timber, raises crops or catches the rain that drains toward a river. Land use is the word for what happens on a piece of land: the benefits people take from it and the work they do there. This chapter follows those choices through forests, farms and water, starting with forestry, the craft of growing, using and repairing forests. It then goes underground, to the water held in the pores of soil and rock, and asks why so many regions lack the fresh water they need. Along the way it meets farms that squeeze ever more from each unit of land, and the web of people and institutions that feeds a population.
